The patient compositor

By J. Marsh · 6 min read

The first commercial letterpress workshops in Britain emerged during the late seventeenth century, clustering near the printing trades along Fleet Street and Paternoster Row. Apprentices learned to set type by hand, sliding individual sorts into a composing stick before transferring entire lines into a galley tray. Their progress was measured not by speed alone but by the cleanliness of the printed sheet, the evenness of the impression, and the patience required to reset a single careless mistake.

A skilled compositor could ordinarily handle around one thousand letters in an hour, distributing them across two cases held at waist height. The upper case contained capitals, small caps, and rarely used glyphs; the lower case held the everyday letterforms, ligatures, and standard punctuation. Speed mattered, but accuracy mattered more: a single transposed slug could throw a paragraph out of register and force the entire form to be unlocked, corrected, and reassembled before the press would run.

Inking was its own quiet skill. The pressman would charge a leather ball or, later, a roller with stiff oil-based ink, then dab it onto the locked form with a rhythm that left no streaks. Too little ink and the impression looked anaemic; too much and the counters of the letters filled in, blurring every serif. Experienced printers could read the colour of a sheet across the room and adjust their stroke before another bad copy was ever pulled.
